articles.body: 1Password was breached through one GitHub account. I built a CLI that traces whether yours can walk alone from push to production. On 25 November 2026, 1Password disclosed a security incident. An attacker used one employee's corporate GitHub account to access source code, push malicious code to backend services, and download admin data for a subset of customers: names, emails, identifiers, SRP parameters, and invite, provisioning and recovery tokens. The investigation began on 19 November. Vault contents were not accessed. Credentials were rotated, and invite and recovery codes were lengthened from 6 numeric digits to 10 alphanumeric characters. Read that again slowly. One account. No second credential was needed.

articles.title: Your AI Monitor Shares a GPU With the Agent It Watches. Here Is How to Separate Them
articles.excerpt: A common safety setup for AI agents looks like this: one model does the work, and a second model reviews each action before it runs. If the reviewer sees something suspicious, it blocks the action. To…
articles.body: A common safety setup for AI agents looks like this: one model does the work, and a second model reviews each action before it runs. If the reviewer sees something suspicious, it blocks the action. To check that the reviewer is honest, you mix in fake suspicious actions (honeypots) and confirm it catches them. Now put both models on the same inference server, because that is cheaper. According to a new research post on LessWrong , that shared server is enough for the two models to talk. In the author's test, a monitor fine-tuned to collude let through 354 of 354 real attacks while still catching 85 to 92% of honeypots, about the same rate as an honest monitor. It never flagged a benign action, so from the outside it looked like a good reviewer.

articles.body: Ordering from memory usually means ordering too much of what you already have and missing what is about to run out. In my November 2026 inventory sample, the closing stock is 1,249 units worth 50,227,000 VND, and 3 items are already flagged low stock. The overview sheet gathers those flagged items into one list, so the next order starts from that list instead of from a walk past the shelves. Two habits keep that list trustworthy: record every stock-in and stock-out on the day it happens, one row at a time; and read the low-stock list together with the best sellers — Coca 63, Sugar 55, Gummy candy 50, Bottled water 48, Rice 43 in the sample — before deciding quantities. Do you order from a low-stock list, or from what the shelf looks like?

articles.title: The 100 KB photo limit: why application forms ask for it, and how to hit it
articles.excerpt: Visa applications. Passport photos. A university portal. A job site. A marketplace listing. A government form that has been online since 2009. Sooner or later one of them tells you something like this…
articles.body: Visa applications. Passport photos. A university portal. A job site. A marketplace listing. A government form that has been online since 2009. Sooner or later one of them tells you something like this: Photo must be JPG, under 100 KB, 413 × 531 pixels. And the photo on your phone is 4 MB and 4032 pixels wide. I build small Android apps on my own, and this is the exact problem my latest one exists for. Here is what I learned about these limits while building it — useful whether you use my app or not. Where the limits come from Nothing about 100 KB is sacred. It is just what the form's back end was built to accept, and the numbers come from somewhere: Bandwidth and storage. Online visa and government portals take millions of uploads a year. A few hundred KB per file is a cost. Print sizes.

articles.title: The Email That Should Have Been a Five-Minute Call
articles.excerpt: Everyone knows the joke about the meeting that could have been an email. It's on mugs. People say it in standups with a knowing look. Nobody has a mug for the opposite: the email that should have been…
articles.body: Everyone knows the joke about the meeting that could have been an email. It's on mugs. People say it in standups with a knowing look. Nobody has a mug for the opposite: the email that should have been a five-minute call. You've been in one. It starts with a simple question. Someone replies with half an answer. Someone else adds a manager. A fourth person replies to the second message, not the latest one, so now there are two threads pretending to be one. By message 9 someone asks what we're actually trying to decide. By message 14 it's mid-afternoon, nothing is decided, and three people have spent their focus time rereading the same paragraph. I've lost days both ways, as a developer, a tech lead and now a team lead. Bad meetings are easy to see because they sit on your calendar.

You’d be surprised to learn that memory costs have gone from accounting for 13% of a phone’s total component costs in early 2025 to more than 40% by late 2026. articles.title: December full moon 2026: When, where and how to see the Cold Moon
articles.excerpt: Your guide to December's full Cold Moon, from peak times to skywatching highlights.
articles.body: The December full moon reaches peak illumination at 8:28 p.m. EST on Dec. 23 (0128 GMT on Dec. 24) as the lunar disk shines opposite the sun in Earth's sky. It is often called the "Cold Moon" in reference to the frigid temperatures that prevail in the Northern Hemisphere around the time of its rising, according to the Old Farmer's Almanac . December's full moon will also occur close to perigee — the moon's closest point to Earth in its elliptical orbit — giving rise to a spectacular supermoon. A supermoon can appear 30% brighter and 14% larger than a full moon at its farthest point from Earth (also known as a micromoon)..

articles.title: On this day in space! Nov. 25, 1970: NASA's 'wingless' M2-F3 'lifting body' aircraft makes its 1st powered flight ahead of supersonic tests
articles.excerpt: On Nov. 25, 1970, an experimental aircraft called the Northrop M2-F3 made its first powered flight. Here's why it mattered.
articles.body: On Nov. 25, 1970, an experimental aircraft called the Northrop M2-F3 made its first powered flight. The M2-F3 aircraft was a heavyweight "lifting body" designed to test its ability to produce most of its lift through its fuselage instead of wings. It's commonly referred to as a "wingless" aircraft. After Air Force test pilot Bill Dana took the M2-F3 on three unpowered glide test flights, he did the first powered flight, too. Dana soared to an altitude of 45,000 feet during this flight, which lasted just over 6 minutes. He didn't break the sound barrier this time, but he did on later flights. The M2-F3 flew a total of 27 missions in its three-year flight history. Its top speed was 1.6 times the speed of sound, and its top altitude was 71,500 feet.
